title: Programming Basics + DSA Fundamentals
subject: Programming
description: A foundation pack extended with four core DSA topics: arrays, hashing, stacks, and binary search.

concepts.title: Variables
concepts.summary: A variable is a name that holds a value.

explanations.plain: A variable is a name that points to a value. x = 5 stores 5 under the name x.
explanations.worked-example: If score = 8 and then score = score + 2 runs, the old value 8 is read, 2 is added, and score now stores 10.

teachBack.label: a variable is a name for a stored value

concepts.title: Lists
concepts.summary: A list holds many values in order. Positions start at 0.

explanations.plain: A list keeps several values in order. The first item is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on.
explanations.worked-example: For colors = ['red', 'blue', 'green'], colors[0] is 'red' and colors[2] is 'green'. The list has 3 items, so its final index is 2.

teachBack.label: the first item is at index 0
items keep their order

concepts.title: Loops
concepts.summary: A loop repeats a block of code.

explanations.plain: A for loop repeats its body once for each value it is given, for example each value from range().
explanations.worked-example: for n in [2, 4, 6] runs its body three times. The values of n are 2, then 4, then 6.

teachBack.label: a loop repeats code

concepts.title: Loop bounds
concepts.summary: range(a, b) starts at a and stops before b.

explanations.plain: range(a, b) gives the numbers from a up to, but not including, b. A list starts at index 0, so a loop over every item usually starts at 0.
explanations.counterexample: Try range(1, 3) on [4, 7, 2]. i is 1, then 2. The 4 at index 0 is never visited.

teachBack.label: where the loop starts (the first value of i)
the stop value is not included
list positions start at 0

concepts.title: Functions
concepts.summary: A function is a reusable block of code with a name.

explanations.plain: A function packages code under a name so you can run it again by calling it.
explanations.worked-example: def double(n): return n * 2 defines a function. Calling double(4) runs its body with n = 4 and returns 8.

teachBack.label: a function is a named block of code
calling a function runs it
a function can return a value

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A function that calls itself, with a base case to stop.

explanations.plain: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem and stops at a base case.
explanations.worked-example: To count down from 3, calls receive 3, then 2, then 1, then 0. The base case at 0 stops and returns instead of calling again.

teachBack.label: a recursive function calls itself
a base case stops the recursion
each recursive step solves a smaller problem

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.summary: An array stores many values in ordered slots so we can read and update each item by index.

explanations.plain: Arrays keep values in fixed positions. We access each item using its index, and the first slot is at index 0.
explanations.worked-example: If nums = [10, 20, 30], then nums[0] is 10, nums[1] is 20, and nums[2] is 30.

teachBack.label: an array item is selected by its index
the array keeps the original order unless we change an item
the first array index is 0

concepts.title: Hashing
concepts.summary: Hashing maps a key to a value so lookups are fast and direct.

explanations.plain: A hash map stores values under unique keys, so we can find a value by key in almost constant time.
explanations.worked-example: The map {'alice': 95, 'bob': 87} lets us ask for scores['alice'] and get 95.

teachBack.label: a hash map connects a key to a value
lookups use the key to find the value quickly
each key identifies one stored value

concepts.title: Stacks
concepts.summary: A stack follows LIFO: the last item added is removed first.

explanations.plain: A stack adds items on top and removes the most recently added item first. This is called LIFO.
explanations.analogy: A stack is like a pile of plates: you put a new plate on top and the top plate comes off first.

teachBack.label: the top item is the most recent one
a stack follows last in, first out
push adds; pop removes the top item

concepts.title: Binary Search
concepts.summary: Binary search repeatedly cuts a sorted list in half until it finds the target or proves it is missing.

explanations.plain: Binary search works only on sorted data. It checks the middle item, discards half the list, and keeps searching on the remaining half.
explanations.worked-example: In [2, 5, 9, 15, 28], the middle is 9. If the target is 15, the search moves to the right half.

teachBack.label: binary search assumes the data is sorted
it chooses the middle element each time
it removes half the remaining space each step

misconceptions.title: Off-by-one (loop start)
misconceptions.description: thinks a loop starting at 1 still visits the item at index 0

explanations.plain: Index 0 is the first item. A loop that starts at 1 skips it.

misconceptions.title: Off-by-one (loop end)
misconceptions.description: thinks the stop value of range() is included

explanations.plain: The stop value of range() is never included.

misconceptions.title: Index and value confused
misconceptions.description: mixes up the position i with the value nums[i]

explanations.plain: i is the position. nums[i] is the value stored there.

misconceptions.title: Range read as 'first n items'
misconceptions.description: thinks range(a, b) means the first b-a items from the start

explanations.plain: range(a, b) starts at a, not at the beginning of the list.

misconceptions.title: Shifted range
misconceptions.description: shifts both ends of range() by one

explanations.plain: Shifting both ends reaches an index that does not exist and still skips index 0.

misconceptions.title: Index starts at 1
misconceptions.description: thinks the first list item is at index 1

explanations.plain: In Python the first item is at index 0.

misconceptions.title: Length equals last index
misconceptions.description: thinks len(list) is the index of the last item

explanations.plain: A list of 3 items has indexes 0, 1, 2. The last index is len - 1.

misconceptions.title: range starts at 1
misconceptions.description: thinks range(n) produces 1 to n

explanations.plain: range(n) produces 0 up to n - 1.

misconceptions.title: Runs = stop value
misconceptions.description: thinks the body runs as many times as the stop value

explanations.plain: range(a, b) runs b - a times.

misconceptions.title: Index offset
misconceptions.description: thinks the first array item is at index 1 instead of 0

explanations.plain: Arrays use zero-based indexing, so the first item is at 0.

misconceptions.title: Array length mistaken for value
misconceptions.description: mistakes the length of the array for an item or an index

explanations.plain: Length tells how many items there are. The last valid index is length minus one.

misconceptions.title: Lookup and position mix-up
misconceptions.description: reads the wrong slot when picking an array position

explanations.plain: Each item is stored at its own index, so the position you ask for decides which value you get.

misconceptions.title: Key and value swapped
misconceptions.description: thinks a dictionary returns the key when you ask for the value

explanations.plain: A dictionary returns the value stored under the key, not the key itself.

misconceptions.title: Wrong lookup result
misconceptions.description: chooses a different key's value instead of the requested one

explanations.plain: Lookups are matched by the exact key in the map, not by the last item or a nearby key.

misconceptions.title: Missing default confusion
misconceptions.description: forgets that get(key, default) returns the default when the key is absent

explanations.plain: If a key is missing, the default is returned unless the key is present.

misconceptions.title: LIFO mistaken
misconceptions.description: thinks the first pushed value comes out first instead of the newest one

explanations.plain: Stacks remove the last item added, so they follow last-in-first-out.

misconceptions.title: Top item guess
misconceptions.description: picks some other item instead of the top of the stack

explanations.plain: The top of a stack is always the most recently added item.

misconceptions.title: Push/pop mix-up
misconceptions.description: forgets that pop removes the current top item

explanations.plain: push adds one item, and pop removes the current top item.

misconceptions.title: Middle choice mistake
misconceptions.description: picks the wrong middle index instead of the center slot

explanations.plain: Binary search always checks the middle element, using the current low and high bounds.

misconceptions.title: Half-range mistake
misconceptions.description: searches the wrong half after learning the middle value

explanations.plain: If the target is larger than the middle, search the right half; if smaller, search the left half.

misconceptions.title: Sorted data forgotten
misconceptions.description: forgets that binary search only works when data is sorted

explanations.plain: Binary search relies on the array being sorted so the correct half can be discarded safely.

misconceptions.title: Assignment is not a formula
misconceptions.description: thinks a variable keeps the old value instead of updating to the new expression

explanations.plain: When you assign a variable, its value becomes the result of the right-hand side at that moment.

misconceptions.title: Name and value confused
misconceptions.description: confuses the variable name with the value stored inside it

explanations.plain: The variable name is just a label. The value is the data currently stored there.

misconceptions.title: Return value confused
misconceptions.description: thinks the function body itself is the output instead of the returned value

explanations.plain: A function may produce a value with return, and that value is what callers receive.

misconceptions.title: Function call skipped
misconceptions.description: forgets that a function only runs when it is called

explanations.plain: Defining a function does not execute it. You must call it to run its code.

misconceptions.title: Base case forgotten
misconceptions.description: forgets that recursion needs a stop condition

explanations.plain: Without a base case, the function keeps calling itself forever or until it crashes.

misconceptions.title: Recursive step not smaller
misconceptions.description: keeps calling the function on the same size problem instead of reducing it

explanations.plain: Each recursive step must move toward the base case by making the problem smaller.

misconceptions.title: Accumulator starts at one
misconceptions.description: adds an extra one by initializing a running total incorrectly

explanations.plain: This running total starts at 0 and then adds each value once.

misconceptions.title: First value counted twice
misconceptions.description: initializes a running total with the first value and then adds that value again in the loop

explanations.plain: Start the total at 0 when the loop will add every list item.

misconceptions.title: Running total reset
misconceptions.description: forgets that the accumulator keeps its previous value between loop passes

explanations.plain: An accumulator keeps the sum so far and adds the next value to it.

misconceptions.title: Loop includes the length
misconceptions.description: uses a loop condition that lets the index equal the list length

explanations.plain: A list of length n has valid indexes only from 0 through n - 1.

misconceptions.title: Loop stops too early
misconceptions.description: stops before visiting the final valid list index

explanations.plain: Use a condition that remains true for the final valid index, len(values) - 1.

misconceptions.title: Loop condition is false initially
misconceptions.description: chooses a condition that is false for the initial index of zero

explanations.plain: Check the condition with the initial value of i before tracing the loop body.

misconceptions.title: Index printed instead of item
misconceptions.description: reports the position number instead of the value stored at that position

explanations.plain: The index is a position; values[index] gives the item stored at that position.

misconceptions.title: First item skipped
misconceptions.description: starts a traversal at index one and misses the item at index zero

explanations.plain: A traversal from index 0 includes the first item in the list.

misconceptions.title: Length used as an item
misconceptions.description: confuses the number of list items with the values stored in the list

explanations.plain: len(values) counts the items; values[i] reads one of those items.

misconceptions.title: Base case stops too early
misconceptions.description: stops before the recursive calculation has included all values down to zero

explanations.plain: Trace which values are included before deciding where the base case should stop.

misconceptions.title: Base case points the wrong way
misconceptions.description: chooses a stopping condition that is already true at the initial input

explanations.plain: A base case should stop when the recursive input reaches the intended smallest problem.

questions.prompt: What is nums[1]?
hints: Which index is the first item?

index-starts-at-one.plain: nums[1] is the SECOND item, because the first item is nums[0].

len-is-last-index.plain: nums[2] is the last item. nums[1] is the middle one, which is 6.

array-length-misread.plain: The length is 3, but nums[1] is the second element in the list, which is 6.

questions.prompt: Which index is the last item?
hints: Count the indexes starting from 0.

len-is-last-index.plain: len(nums) is 3, but indexes run 0, 1, 2. The last index is len(nums) - 1.

index-starts-at-one.plain: Index 1 is the middle item. Indexes run 0, 1, 2.

array-index-offset.plain: The first item is at index 0. The last item is the third item, which is at index 2.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
hints: What is the first value of i?

off-by-one-end.plain: The stop value 3 is not included, so the last value is 2.

counts-from-zero.plain: The values go upward from 0 to 2, not backward from 2 to 0.

questions.prompt: How many times does the loop body run?
hints: List every value of i.

off-by-one-end.plain: i takes 2, 3, 4, 5. The stop value 6 is not included, so 4 runs.

count-equals-stop.plain: The count is stop minus start: 6 - 2 = 4, not 6.

counts-from-zero.plain: The loop starts at 2, not at 0, and it stops before 6.

questions.prompt: Which value is at index 1?
hints: Count from zero.

array-index-offset.plain: The first item is at index 0, so index 1 is the second item: 4.

array-lookup-mixup.plain: 7 is the third item, which is at index 2, not index 1.

array-length-misread.plain: The array length is 3, but index 1 points to the second element, which is 4.

questions.prompt: After `nums.append(12)` and `nums.pop()`, what is the value at index 2?
hints: The last item is removed, then the array stays in order.

array-lookup-mixup.plain: The appended value is removed before the final check, so index 2 is still 9.

array-index-offset.plain: The item at index 2 is the third element, which remains 9 after the pop.

array-length-misread.plain: Length tells the number of items, but the third value is still 9 because the last element was removed.

questions.prompt: If `nums = [5, 11, 17, 23]` and `nums[1] = 8`, what is `nums[3]`?
hints: Only one slot changes.

array-lookup-mixup.plain: Changing index 1 does not change the value at index 3, which remains 23.

array-index-offset.plain: The old value at index 1 was 11, but index 3 still points to 23.

array-length-misread.plain: The length is 4, but index 3 is still the fourth item, which is 23.

questions.prompt: What is `scores['alice']`?
hints: Ask for the value stored under the key.

hash-key-value-swap.plain: The dictionary returns the value 95 for the key 'alice', not the key itself.

hash-lookup-misread.plain: The key 'alice' matches the value 95, not the other key 'bob'.

hash-missing-default-confusion.plain: The key is present, so the dictionary returns 95 instead of raising an error.

questions.prompt: What is `counts['a']` after this code?
hints: Increment the existing value for the same key.

hash-lookup-misread.plain: The key 'a' is updated from 2 to 3, so its value becomes 3.

hash-key-value-swap.plain: The value is increased, not replaced by the key name or by a different key.

hash-missing-default-confusion.plain: No default is used here; the value under the key 'a' is updated to 3.

questions.prompt: What does `seen.get('green', 0)` return?
hints: When a key is not present, the default is returned.

hash-lookup-misread.plain: The key 'green' is not in the dictionary, so the default 0 is used.

hash-missing-default-confusion.plain: get(key, default) returns the default value, not None, when the key isn't present.

hash-key-value-swap.plain: The dictionary does not return a random stored value; it returns the default 0 because 'green' is missing.

questions.prompt: What does this pop from the stack?
hints: A stack removes the most recently added item.

stack-lifo-confused.plain: Stacks are LIFO, so the most recent item 'B' comes off first.

stack-top-guess.plain: pop removes the item at the top, which is 'B'.

stack-pop-miscall.plain: A stack does not invent a new item; it removes the top item, which is 'B'.

questions.prompt: After these operations, what is the stack content?
hints: Pop removes the current top item, then push adds a new one.

stack-lifo-confused.plain: The top item 'B' is popped before 'C' is pushed. The remaining stack is ['A', 'C'].

stack-pop-miscall.plain: A pop removes the top item, so 'B' is removed before 'C' is added.

stack-top-guess.plain: The stack still contains 'A' after the pop, and then 'C' is pushed on top.

questions.prompt: Which item will be removed next?
questions.code:
stack = ['A', 'B', 'C']
# C was pushed most recently
hints: In a stack the newest item is at the top.

stack-lifo-confused.plain: A stack removes the newest item, not the oldest one. So C comes off first.

stack-top-guess.plain: The top item is the most recently added one, which is C.

stack-pop-miscall.plain: A stack still has a top item to remove. The next one out is C.

questions.prompt: In a sorted list `[3, 7, 11, 19, 25]`, which index is checked first in binary search?
hints: Binary search checks the middle element first.

binary-middle-choice.plain: The middle index of a 5-item list is 2, not 0.

binary-half-ignore.plain: The first step always starts in the middle, which is index 2.

binary-sorted-assumption.plain: Binary search starts at the middle item, so index 2 is checked before either end.

questions.prompt: Given `nums = [3, 7, 11, 19, 25]` and target `19`, what should the next search range be after checking the middle item `11`?
hints: If the target is larger than the middle, keep the right half.

binary-half-ignore.plain: 19 is larger than 11, so the search moves to the right half: indices 3 and 4.

binary-middle-choice.plain: The middle index 2 is already checked. The next interval is the right half, not the full range.

binary-sorted-assumption.plain: Binary search does not keep the whole array after the midpoint. It discards the left half because the target is larger than the midpoint.

questions.prompt: Why is binary search valid for this task?

options.text: The list is sorted, so the search can discard half the data each step.
It works on any list, even if it is unsorted.
It checks the first item first and then moves right.
It only works when the list has an even length.

hints: Binary search needs a clear order before dividing.

binary-sorted-assumption.plain: Binary search depends on a sorted list so it can safely discard half of the remaining candidates.

binary-middle-choice.plain: The algorithm starts at the middle, not the first item.

binary-half-ignore.plain: The search can work with odd or even lengths as long as the list is sorted and the middle is chosen correctly.

questions.prompt: What is x after this code runs?
hints: Update the variable using the current value.

variable-reassign-mistake.plain: The new value is calculated from the current value 5 plus 2, so x becomes 7.

variable-name-vs-value.plain: x is a label for the stored value, and the stored value becomes 7 after the assignment.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
hints: The function returns a value after the call.

function-call-omitted.plain: The function is called with 4, so it computes 4 + 1 and returns 5.

function-return-confused.plain: The expression x + 1 is the calculation, and the function returns the final value 5.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `fact(3)`?
hints: The base case stops the recursion at 0.

recursive-step-size-wrong.plain: Each call reduces n by 1 until it reaches the base case 0, producing 6.

questions.prompt: What are x and y after these assignments?

options.text: x and y both refer to the name x

hints: Assignments copy the current value on the right into the variable on the left.

variable-reassign-mistake.plain: When y = x runs, x is 4, so y receives 4. Changing x later does not change y.

variable-name-vs-value.plain: x and y are separate names. At the end, x stores 9 and y stores 4.

questions.prompt: What is the final value of total?
hints: Evaluate each assignment from top to bottom.

variable-reassign-mistake.plain: step becomes 3 + 2 = 5, then total is reassigned to 5 * 2 = 10.

variable-name-vs-value.plain: The expression uses the stored value of step, which is 5; the final total is 10.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
hints: Find b when its assignment runs; later assignments to a do not recalculate b.

variable-reassign-mistake.plain: b is assigned 6 + 1 = 7 before a changes to 2.

variable-name-vs-value.plain: b stores the result of its assignment, 7; it does not remain linked to the name a.

questions.prompt: What are values[0] and values[-1]?
hints: Index 0 is the first item; index -1 is the last item.

index-starts-at-one.plain: Index 0 selects the first item, 12. Index -1 selects the last item, 31.

len-is-last-index.plain: The length is 4, but values[-1] means the last item, which is 31.

lists-index-vs-value.plain: The values at the requested positions are 12 and 31; the positions themselves are not printed.

questions.prompt: What is the value of total after the loop?
hints: range(2, 5) produces 2, 3, and 4.

count-equals-stop.plain: The loop runs three times with values 2, 3, and 4, so their sum is 9.

range-counts-from-one.plain: The values begin at 2, not 1, and the stop value 5 is excluded.

questions.prompt: Which values does range(2, 6) produce?
hints: The first value is included; the stop value is not.

off-by-one-end.plain: The stop value 6 is excluded, so the final value is 5.

counts-from-zero.plain: The range starts at 2, not at zero.

off-by-one-start.plain: The start value 2 is included as the first value.

questions.prompt: How many times does the loop run?
hints: List the values: 3, 5, 7, ... and stop before 10.

off-by-one-end.plain: The values are 3, 5, 7, and 9. The stop value 10 is not included, giving four runs.

off-by-one-start.plain: The start value 3 is included; the values are 3, 5, 7, and 9.

counts-from-zero.plain: The step is 2 and the start is 3, so the loop visits four values before reaching or passing 10.

questions.prompt: What does this call return?
hints: Substitute 3 for a and 4 for b in the return expression.

function-return-confused.plain: The function returns a * 10 + b, which is 3 * 10 + 4 = 34.

function-call-omitted.plain: The call supplies a = 3 and b = 4; the expression keeps their positions, so it returns 34.

questions.prompt: What is printed?
questions.code:
def add(a, b):
    result = a + b
    return result
x = add(2, 5)
print(x * 2)
hints: First evaluate the function call, then evaluate the print expression.

function-return-confused.plain: add(2, 5) returns 7, which is stored in x; print then outputs 7 * 2 = 14.

function-call-omitted.plain: The function call returns 7, and the code then multiplies that returned value by 2.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
def change(n):
    n = n + 3
    return n
value = 4
print(change(value), value)
hints: The function parameter n is local to the call; value is not reassigned.

function-return-confused.plain: change(value) returns 7, but changing its local parameter n does not reassign value, which remains 4.

function-call-omitted.plain: change(value) is called and returns 7; value itself remains 4.

questions.prompt: What does sum_down(3) return?
hints: Expand the calls: 3 + sum_down(2), then continue until n is 0.

recursive-base-case-missed.plain: The calls add 3 + 2 + 1, then the base case returns 0, for a total of 6.

recursive-step-size-wrong.plain: Each call contributes its current n before calling n - 1; the total is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

recursive-base-case-too-early.plain: Stopping at n = 1 before adding it leaves only 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.prompt: What does factorial(4) return?
hints: Expand 4 * factorial(3) until the base case is reached.

recursive-base-case-missed.plain: The base case returns 1 at n = 1, after 4, 3, and 2 have been multiplied.

recursive-base-case-too-early.plain: The base case returns 1 rather than 0, and the earlier calls multiply to 24.

questions.prompt: What is nums[2] after this update?
hints: An assignment to nums[2] replaces the item at index 2.

array-lookup-mixup.plain: Index 2 is updated from 14 to 17, so nums[2] is now 17.

array-length-misread.plain: The index is a position, not the stored value; nums[2] contains 17 after the update.

array-index-offset.plain: Indexes start at 0, and the assignment directly sets the value at index 2 to 17.

questions.prompt: What is scores['maya'] after the update?
hints: Find Maya's current value, then add 5 to that value.

hash-lookup-misread.plain: The update adds 5 to Maya's stored value 84, giving 89.

hash-key-value-swap.plain: 'maya' is the key; its value changes from 84 to 89.

hash-missing-default-confusion.plain: The key already exists, so its value 84 is updated to 89.

questions.prompt: What value does the final pop return?

options.text: The stack is empty before the final pop

hints: After each pop, remove only the current top item.

stack-lifo-confused.plain: The first pop removes green. Blue is then pushed on top and is removed by the final pop.

stack-top-guess.plain: Red remains at the bottom after the first pop; blue is added above it and comes off first.

stack-pop-miscall.plain: The stack contains red after the first pop, then blue is pushed, so the final pop returns blue.

questions.prompt: After checking index 3, what range remains when searching for 24?
hints: The target is greater than the value at index 3, so keep only indexes to its right.

binary-half-ignore.plain: 24 is greater than nums[3] = 16, so continue in the right half at indexes 4 through 6.

binary-middle-choice.plain: Index 3 has already been checked; the remaining right-side indexes are 4 through 6.

binary-sorted-assumption.plain: Because the list is sorted, values left of index 3 can be discarded; search indexes 4 through 6.
